## Executive Summary

Token management in multi-agent LLM systems is a three-dimensional problem:
**budget** (how many tokens each agent can use), **context** (how to use the
available window effectively), and **cost** (how to track and control spending).

Key findings:

- **Context windows are smaller than advertised.** Effective context is 60-70%
  of the advertised maximum [45]. Performance degrades 13.9%-85% as input
  length increases even with perfect information retrieval [6]. The practical
  ceiling is ~80% of the context window [13][29].

- **Token budgeting has formal foundations.** The Agent Contracts framework [1]
  establishes conservation laws for hierarchical token allocation, achieving 90%
  token reduction with 525× lower variance in controlled experiments.

- **Cost compounds multiplicatively in multi-agent systems.** Three parallel
  agents with fan-out can burn $2,250/day [23]. Token usage accounts for 80%
  of performance variance in multi-agent architectures [28].

- **Prevention beats recovery.** Memory pointers [5] and programmatic tool
  calling [22] keep large data out of context entirely. This is more effective
  than compression (26-54% [3]), summarization (which risks trajectory
  elongation [56]), or truncation (which loses information).

- **Prompt caching is the highest-ROI optimization.** Cache reads cost 0.1×
  base input price (90% savings) with Anthropic [17]. Combined with batching
  and routing, total savings reach 70-90% [55].

- **LangGraph checkpointing replaces legacy memory.** Thread-scoped persistence
  via checkpointers is the current recommendation for all new agent
  implementations [20]. Pair with Mem0 for cross-session memory (26% accuracy
  gains over plain vector approaches) [52].

## Token Budget Allocation Patterns

### Per-Agent Limits

The simplest pattern: each agent receives a fixed token allocation. LangGraph
supports explicit token/time budgets in orchestration configuration. AutoGen
provides inference and optimization budgets measured in dollars per 1K tokens
[34]. CrewAI offers `respect_context_window` and `max_tokens` parameters [33].

The limitation: unused allocation from one agent cannot benefit another [1].

### Shared Budgets and Token Pools

Token pools express capacity through three schedulable resources: token
throughput (tokens/second), KV cache capacity (bytes), and request concurrency
[4]. Key features:

- Burst absorption by reallocating unused tokens [4]
- Service debt for fairness — accumulated under-allocation creates
  compensatory priority [4]
- Cross-class protection: sub-1.2s P99 latency for guaranteed workloads during
  38% overload, vs 19s baseline degradation [4]

### Conservation Laws

The Agent Contracts framework [1] establishes a fundamental invariant:

> ∑(consumption by each agent) ≤ B(resource) for all resources

Three strategies: proportional (by estimated complexity), equal (when
complexity unknown), and negotiated (agents request with coordinator caps) [1].
Dynamic reallocation returns unused budget from completed agents to a shared
pool [1].

### Empirical Results

| Method | Token Reduction | Accuracy Impact |
|--------|----------------|-----------------|
| Agent Contracts (code review) | 90% | Equivalent quality [1] |
| TALE framework | 68.64% output tokens | < 3% decline [2] |
| Hierarchical architecture | 39.1% cost reduction | 97.7% of best accuracy [28] |
| Context isolation (subagents) | 67% fewer tokens | — [28] |

**Fundamental limitation**: Token consumption is known only after LLM calls
complete, not during generation. Contracts cannot prevent a single expensive call
from exceeding budget, only prevent subsequent calls [1].

## Context Window Management Strategies

### Strategy Comparison

| Strategy | Token Savings | Quality Risk | Best For |
|----------|-------------|--------------|----------|
| Memory pointers | Up to 99.99% [5] | None (full data preserved) | Large tool outputs |
| PTC (Anthropic) | 37% [22] | None (result filtering) | 3+ dependent tool calls |
| ACON compression | 26-54% [3] | 5% accuracy loss [3] | Long-horizon agents |
| Prompt caching | N/A (cost reduction) | None | Repetitive prefixes |
| Summarization | Moderate | Trajectory elongation risk [56] | Medium conversations |
| RAG | High | Retrieval quality dependent | Large knowledge bases |
| Truncation | High | Information loss | Last resort |

### Memory Pointers (Best for Large Tool Outputs)

Store large outputs externally, pass short references [5]:
- Molecular Grid Retrieval: ~1,234 tokens vs ~20.8M (conventional infeasible)
- Safety Data Sheet: 842 vs 6,411 tokens (~7× reduction)
- Framework-agnostic, no changes to LLMs or tools required

### Programmatic Tool Calling (Best for Multi-Step Workflows)

Claude writes Python code orchestrating tools in sandboxed execution; only
final output returns to context [22]:
- 37% reduction on complex research tasks (43,588 → 27,297 tokens)
- Budget compliance: 200KB raw data → 1KB results

### Prompt Caching (Best for Cost Reduction)

Anthropic cache reads: 0.1× base input price (90% savings) [17]. Minimum
cacheable: 1,024-4,096 tokens depending on model. Multi-turn conversation:
~80% savings after first turn. Combined with batching: 95%+ savings [55].

### RAG vs Long Context

LC generally outperforms RAG in QA benchmarks. RAG excels at fragmented
information and dialogue contexts. Speed: RAG ~1s vs LC 30-60s [10].
Summarization-based retrieval performs comparably to LC; chunk-based retrieval
significantly underperforms [10].

### Warning: Summarization Risk

Summarization can cause "trajectory elongation" — smoothing over failure
severity causes agents to miss being stuck [56]. Observation masking (preserving
failure signals while removing token-heavy output) is preferable for agent
tasks [56].

See [references/context-window-management.md](references/context-window-management.md)
for full analysis.

<a name="token-counting"></a>
## Token Counting: Tools, Accuracy, and Cross-Provider Challenges

### Provider APIs

| Provider | Method | Accuracy | Cost |
|----------|--------|----------|------|
| Anthropic | Server-side API [14] | Estimate (may include unbilled system tokens) | Free |
| OpenAI | tiktoken (client-side) [15] | Estimate (+3/msg, +3 reply, +7-10/function) | Free |
| Google | Server-side API [16] | Estimate (multimodal approximate) | Free |
| AWS Bedrock | Server-side API [26] | Model-specific | Free |

**The "1 token ≈ 4 characters" rule is only a rough estimate** [16]. Factors
that inflate counts: URLs (15+ tokens), JSON (~2× vs text), base64 (10-50×),
non-English text [15].

### Cross-Provider Challenges

Different providers use different tokenizers. Identical text produces different
token counts (e.g., OpenAI 15 tokens where Claude counts 17). Langfuse notes
that the Anthropic tokenizer is "not accurate for Claude 3 models" — use API
response tokens when possible [24].

### Accuracy Hierarchy

1. Provider API response (`usage.prompt_tokens`) — billing ground truth
2. Provider token counting API — pre-send estimate
3. Provider-specific client library (tiktoken) — same-provider only
4. Cross-provider libraries (tokencost, 400+ models [31]) — estimate
5. Character heuristic (÷4) — rough planning only

See [references/token-counting-tools.md](references/token-counting-tools.md)
for full analysis.

## Cost Tracking and Control

### The Cost Problem

3 parallel agents × 5 sub-calls × 50K tokens × $0.015/1K = $11.25/round.
At 20 rounds per batch and 10 batches/day: **$2,250/day** [23]. A documented
$47,000 API bill resulted from an uncontrolled multi-agent system [1].

### Three-Layer Governance

**Layer 1: Per-Action** — cap tokens per LLM call, enforce timeouts [23]

**Layer 2: Per-Agent** — time-windowed budgets (research: $50/hour) [23]

**Layer 3: Fleet-Level** — graduated responses [23]:

| Budget Used | Action |
|-------------|--------|
| 50% | Alerts |
| 80% | Throttle non-critical agents |
| 95% | Pause all except approved |
| 100% | Block (last resort) |

### Policy-as-Code

Version-controlled YAML policies enforced before execution [23]:
- Throttle rules (20 LLM calls/hour, 3 concurrent max)
- Approval gates (human review for >$50 estimated cost)
- Deny rules (block recursive loops)
- Per-topic timeouts (research 120s, drafting 60s, enrichment 30s)

### Observability Platforms

| Platform | Model | Key Feature | Free Tier |
|----------|-------|-------------|-----------|
| Langfuse | Open source [24] | Predefined tokenizers, OTel | 50K events/month |
| LiteLLM | Open source [38] | Budget enforcement per key/user | Unlimited |
| Helicone | Open source [39] | 50-80ms proxy, 2B+ interactions | 100K requests/month |
| Portkey | Proprietary [37] | 250+ models, 40+ data points | 10K requests |

OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions provide standard schema for token
counts, cost, and model metadata. Request/response as span events (not
attributes) to avoid bloated spans [25].

### Optimization Stack

| Technique | Savings |
|-----------|---------|
| Prompt caching | Up to 90% on reads [17] |
| Batch API | 50%+ [27] |
| Smart routing | 30-85% [61] |
| Combined | 70-90% total [55] |

See [references/cost-tracking-and-control.md](references/cost-tracking-and-control.md)
for full analysis.

## LangChain/LangGraph Memory Patterns

### Current Recommendation: LangGraph Checkpointing

Memory is part of graph state [20]:
- **Thread-scoped** persistence via checkpointers (short-term)
- **Cross-thread** persistence via Store interface (long-term)
- Automatic checkpoint at each invocation with thread ID
- Time-travel debugging and human-in-the-loop support
- PostgreSQL for production; SQLite for development only [59]

### Memory Type Trade-offs

| Type | Token Usage | Context Retention | Cost Profile |
|------|------------|-------------------|-------------|
| Buffer | Linear growth | Complete | High at scale |
| Summary | Reduced | Lossy (risks elongation [56]) | Extra LLM calls |
| Summary Buffer | Controlled | Recent: full, older: summary | Moderate [58] |
| Token Buffer | Fixed | Sliding window, loses older | Predictable [57] |
| Vector-backed | Per-retrieval | Semantic relevance | Infra overhead |

### Long-Term Memory: Mem0 Integration

LangGraph checkpoints handle short-term; Mem0 provides cross-session semantic
memory [52]:
- Three types: semantic (facts), episodic (experiences), procedural (rules)
- 26% accuracy gains over plain vector approaches [52]
- Storage options: profile model (single JSON) vs collection model (multiple
  documents) [20]

### Memory Classification (Human-Inspired)

| Type | What It Stores | Agent Use |
|------|---------------|-----------|
| Semantic | Facts and concepts | User preferences, personalization [20] |
| Episodic | Past experiences | Few-shot examples for learning [20] |
| Procedural | Rules and instructions | System prompt modification [20] |

See [references/langchain-memory-patterns.md](references/langchain-memory-patterns.md)
for full analysis.

<a name="context-overflow"></a>
## Context Overflow: Failure Modes and Recovery

### Failure Modes

| Mode | Symptom | Frequency |
|------|---------|-----------|
| Hard overflow | API error | Detectable, recoverable |
| Soft degradation | Quality loss at 60-80% fill [6][45] | Silent, insidious |
| Context drift | Agent forgets objectives | 65% of enterprise AI failures [29] |
| Trajectory elongation | Stuck in loops after summarization [56] | Agent-specific |
| Lost in the middle | Wrong answers from middle context [7] | Universal |

### Recovery Hierarchy (Preference Order)

1. **Prevent**: Memory pointers [5], PTC [22] — keep large data out
2. **Compress**: ACON (26-54% reduction) [3]
3. **Mask**: Remove observations, keep reasoning history [56]
4. **Summarize**: Compress history (risk of elongation) [56]
5. **Decompose**: Split across agents via TDAG [44]
6. **Truncate**: Drop oldest messages
7. **Fallback**: Switch to larger-context model [19]
8. **Reset**: New session (last resort)

### Proactive Monitoring

- Use ~80% of context window as soft ceiling [13][29]
- Health probes for cognitive state (CDR framework) [29]
- Token pressure guards at configurable thresholds [29]
- Per-topic timeouts as secondary defense [23]

See [references/context-overflow-recovery.md](references/context-overflow-recovery.md)
for full analysis.

## Multi-Provider Routing and Economics

### 2026 Pricing Snapshot

| Tier | Example Models | Input $/MTok | Output $/MTok |
|------|---------------|-------------|--------------|
| Budget | GPT-5 nano, DeepSeek V3.2 | $0.05-0.14 | $0.28-0.40 |
| Mid-range | Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3 Flash | $0.50-1.00 | $3-5 |
| Premium | Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.2 | $1.75-3.00 | $14-15 |
| Frontier | Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.2 Pro | $5-21 | $25-168 |

Output tokens cost 3-5× more than input [27]. Open-source models ~90% cheaper
at equivalent quality [53]. Prices dropping 10-1,000× per year [60].

### OpenRouter Routing

Inverse-square price weighting: a $1/MTok provider gets 9× more traffic than
$3/MTok [18]. Stability filtered (no outages in 30s). Automatic failover on
context length errors, priced at model actually used [19]. 5.5% fee [36].

### Routing Optimization

| Strategy | Savings |
|----------|---------|
| Smart routing | 30-85% [61] |
| Semantic routing | 85% maintaining 95% quality [43] |
| Hybrid routing | 37-46% [61] |
| Model tiering (60% to cheaper) | 50%+ [43] |

### The Cheapest Model Paradox

A more capable model may cost less overall by understanding prompts correctly
on the first attempt and generating concise responses without refinement [27].
Optimize for total cost to achieve outcome, not per-token price.

<a name="performance-benchmarks"></a>
## Performance Benchmarks and Empirical Data

### Context Degrades Performance

| Finding | Magnitude | Source |
|---------|-----------|--------|
| Performance drops with input length | 13.9%-85% even with perfect retrieval | [6] |
| Effective context window | 60-70% of advertised | [45] |
| Lost in the middle | U-shaped: best at start/end | [7] |
| Context rot onset | 250-500 words (first signs) | [13] |
| Practical ceiling | ~80% of window | [13][29] |

### Latency Scales Non-Linearly

Llama-3.1-70B latency increase at 15K words: **719.64%** [9]. Accuracy decline
at same length: only 0.5 percentage points (98.5% → 98%) [9]. The tax is
operational (latency), not cognitive (accuracy) [9].

### RULER: Advertised vs Real

Only half of models claiming 32K+ context maintain satisfactory performance at
32K [8]. Nearly perfect NIAH scores mask large drops on complex tasks [8].

### Diminishing Returns

- **~40% fill**: Where returns start diminishing (task-dependent) [13]
  *(operator review flag: this threshold is derived from a single source
  and should be validated against specific use cases before relying on it
  for production decisions)*
- **60-70%**: Maximum effective context for most models [45]
- **80%**: Recommended production ceiling [29]

See [references/context-performance-benchmarks.md](references/context-performance-benchmarks.md)
for full analysis.

<a name="recommendations"></a>
## Recommendations for Multi-Agent Systems

Based on the evidence above, for a LangGraph-based multi-agent system with
OpenRouter:

### 1. Budget Architecture

- Implement Agent Contracts [1] with conservation laws for hierarchical
  token allocation
- Set per-agent token limits with dynamic reallocation of unused budget
- Track via Langfuse (open source, LangGraph integration, OTel support) [24]
- Enforce three-layer governance: per-action, per-agent, fleet-level [23]

### 2. Context Management

- Use memory pointers [5] for all tool outputs exceeding a configurable
  threshold (start at 5K tokens)
- Apply prompt caching for system prompts and tool definitions (90% savings
  on reads) [17]
- Use observation masking rather than summarization for agent tasks [56]
- Target 80% context utilization as soft ceiling [13][29]

### 3. Token Counting

- Use provider API response tokens as ground truth for billing [14][15][16]
- Use provider counting APIs for pre-send estimation
- Account for hidden overhead: 3 tokens/message (OpenAI), tool definitions,
  system tokens [15]

### 4. Cost Control

- Enable prompt caching on all Anthropic requests [17]
- Route via OpenRouter with model tiering: budget models for simple tasks,
  premium for complex [18]
- Set per-agent time-windowed budgets with graduated enforcement [23]
- Policy-as-code for cost governance (YAML, version-controlled) [23]

### 5. Memory Architecture

- LangGraph checkpointing for short-term, thread-scoped memory [20]
- PostgreSQL backend for production [59]
- Consider Mem0 integration for cross-session personalization [52]
- Token buffer memory when strict budget compliance required [57]

### 6. Overflow Prevention

- Memory pointers and PTC as first line of defense [5][22]
- ACON compression for long-horizon tasks [3]
- TDAG-style task decomposition when single-agent context is insufficient [44]
- OpenRouter model fallbacks for automatic failover [19]

## Limitations

### Methodology

- Sources are predominantly from 2024-2026; this is a fast-moving domain and
  findings may be superseded within months
- Several data points rely on search snippets rather than full-text extraction
  (marked in [citations.md](citations.md))
- Cross-source synthesis claims (combining findings from multiple papers for a
  single conclusion) should be validated independently

### Coverage Gaps

- **Recovery success rates**: No published data on what percentage of context
  overflows are successfully recovered vs requiring session reset
- **Multi-provider tokenization variance**: No benchmarks comparing identical
  text tokenized across providers to quantify billing differences
- **Budget policy testing**: No published methodologies for testing token
  budget allocation policies before production
- **Mid-generation enforcement**: No provider supports interrupting generation
  when a token budget is exceeded — enforcement is always post-call [1]
- **Reasoning token budgeting**: Best practices for o-series and extended
  thinking models are not yet established

### Contradictions

- The 40% context fill inflection point [13] lacks multi-source validation
  and should be treated as hypothesis rather than established threshold
- The "cheapest model paradox" [27] depends heavily on use case and prompt
  quality — no universal formula exists for when it applies
